title: Exploring Public Sequencing Data
text:
Welcome to the Public Sequencing Data day taught by the Bioinformatics core at the Discovery Research Platform for Hidden Cell Biology, today we will go over several different essential topics when it comes to using public data.
During this course you will learn to:

Learn about different types of sequencing
Explore public databases for sequencing data
Download data and quality assess data
Explore and download reference genomes

If you have any questions please contact Daniel Robertson, Heleen de Weerd or Shaun Webb.

title: Exploring Public Sequencing Data
text: For many different types of bioinformatics analysis, we need to use a reference genome to be able to do our work. Sometimes finding and downloading a proper reference genome can be a challenge. How do we find out if the reference genome works for the specific goal that we have? There are many places that reference genomes are available, though there are two main places to look for reference genomes ENSEMBL and National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI)

title: Intro to Linux
text:
One of the first questions people often ask is: Why do I need Linux? If people are familiar with graphical interfaces used for programs in Windows, why do bioinformaticians use command line? The short answer is that command line and Linux are lightweight, highly flexible, and maybe most importantly for research: free. Besides this, many bioinformatics tools are written and used without a graphical interface, which keeps them lightweight. This makes command line knowledge essential for bioinformatic data processing.
Like Windows and macOS, Linux is an operating system. It manages the computer’s hardware and allows you to run applications. There are many different versions (or distributions) of Linux. Some commercial distributions have a paid licence, but many are completely free. One of the most popular choices is Ubuntu, which is free to download, easy to install, and widely used by both beginners and experienced users. It is the also the version of Linux installed on the DRP-HCB servers.
One thing to note is that bioinformaticians are not the only people who use Linux. Linux powers a large proportion of the world’s servers, supercomputers, and cloud computing infrastructure. Many of these systems do not have a graphical user interface. Instead, they are controlled through the command line. By avoiding the overhead of a graphical interface, more memory and processing power are available for running computationally intensive tasks, such as analysing genomic data.

title: Intro to Linux
text:
Bash Shell
If many Linux servers do not have a graphical user interface, how do we interact with them? The answer is through the command line. If you have ever used Command Prompt or PowerShell on Windows, the basic idea is very similar. Instead of clicking buttons and navigating menus, you only use the keyboard, you type commands to tell the computer what you want it to do.
Linux has a specific vocabulary for how to ask for things, it contains a large collection of built-in commands that allow you to perform almost any task. These commands let you navigate through directories, create and edit files, move or copy data, install software, and run programs. While there are many different Linux distributions, the vast majority use the same core commands, so the skills you learn on one distribution are generally transferable to others. Occasionally, there are small differences, but these are usually minor.
The environment in which you type and execute these commands is called a shell. The shell acts as an interpreter between you and the operating system: it reads the command you type, executes it, and displays the results. At first, using the command line can feel unfamiliar because there are no buttons or menus to guide you. Instead, you communicate with the computer using commands and options, much like learning a new language. Throughout this course, you will gradually learn the most useful commands and develop the confidence to navigate the Linux operating system efficiently.

title: Intro to Linux
text:
Connecting
Today, we will connect to one of the DRP servers to start our Linux journey. Connecting to the server is dependent on the machine you are working with. To connect

Both Linux and Mac have a “Terminal”, which is command line and can connect to a server using ssh. By typing in the following in your terminal, you can easily connect to the DRP server.
Replace <UUN> by your own UUN or username.

ssh <UUN>@bifx-core1.bio.ed.ac.uk

For Windows, a tool like MobaXTerm needs to be installed to be able to connect to a server easily. Connecting uses ssh in this case as well. Take a look at the MobaXTerm demo to learn how to connect using ssh. Make sure to use you UUN as your username and the server link as follow:

bifx-core1.bio.ed.ac.uk
You might be asked if you trust the server, make sure to answer yes. Once you’ve entered your password you should connect to the server and see something like the following:
Welcome to Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (GNU/Linux 6.8.0-117-generic x86_64)

 * Documentation:  https://help.ubuntu.com
 * Management:     https://landscape.canonical.com
 * Support:        https://ubuntu.com/pro
################################################################################
THIS DEVICE IS PART OF A PRIVATE NETWORK.

Unauthorised access or use of this equipment is prohibited 
and constitutes an offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
If you are not authorised to use this system, terminate this 
session now.

All activity on this system is monitored and recorded.

Please direct any queries to IS.Helpline@ed.ac.uk.

################################################################################
<UUN>@bifx-core1:~$
This prompt shows that you are logged in to the bifx-core1 bioinformatics server, and that you are in your home directory (which is referred to using the ~ character on Linux systems).
Please see our website for more specific instructions on using the DRP-HCB bioinformatics servers.

title: Intro to Linux
text:
Commands
The basic structure of most Linux command is as followed:
command [option(s)] [argument(s)]

command: the operation or program you want Linux to execute
options (also called flags or switches): modify the way the command works
arguments: filenames or other targets that direct the action of the command

Options and arguments are not always needed for commands to run. If no options or arguments are given, default settings will be used. We can run commands by typing in the command and pressing [ENTER].
Here an example of default behaviour versus using options.
$ date
The command will result in the date will be displayed in BST (British Summer Time). However if we use the -u option:
Note: be aware to put a space between the command and the option
$ date -u
The date will be displayed in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time). So using options we can change the behavior of the command.


 Challenge:

Try to break the command by using other options. What happens?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Run date with -p (date -p), you should get an error telling you what you are doing is invalid.

title: Intro to Linux
text:
Help
While the use of options and arguments makes commands more powerful and flexible, they can be difficult to remember, and can vary between different versions of the command. Luckily, there are several ways to find out what a command does and what options are available for a command. Most commands can be use with the –help or -h option, which will provide a description of the command and the options.
$ date --help
In some cases, commands will not have the –help or -h option. In these cases, man or info might be available. These all work in similar ways, below an example of how to use man.
$ man date
For both man and info, to get out of the information screen, press Q.


 Challenge:

Run the command:

$ date -d '25 Dec' +%j
Using the help options, can you explain what this command has done?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Looking the result of the command, we can already see that this give a number. Look at the %j option in the help of date, it explains in the help that %j gives the number of the day of the year. The 25th of December is the 359th day of the year (unless it is a leap year then it is the 360th day).

title: Intro to Linux
text:
Tips
Working within Linux sometimes means we want to see what we did previous or rerun commands. Using the Arrow Up and Arrow Down keys we can explore and rerun without having to write the whole command again.
There are few shortcuts within our shell that will come in handy whenever we are working within our environments.


 Key points


Ctrl+a or Home will move the caret (or text cursor) to the beginning of the line
Ctrl+e or End will move the caret to the end of the line
Ctrl+k will delete text from the current position of the caret to the end of the line
Ctrl+y or the middle mouse button will paste the last selected text at the caret position
Ctrl+l will clear the terminal
Tab will try to complete your command or filename from the previously typed text.
For example if you want to run bedtools, you can type bedto and press Tab to complete. If there are multiple options, it won’t complete the name. Press Tab twice to see the options available. For example try to type bed and press Tab twice

Be aware that Ctrl+c, which is normally used for copying selected text, will terminate any command that you are currently running. If you want to copy something from the terminal, use the right mouse button to copy.

title: Exploring Public Sequencing Data
text: For many different types of bioinformatics analysis, we need to use a reference genome to be able to do our work. Sometimes finding and downloading a proper reference genome can be a challenge. How do we find out if the reference genome works for the specific goal that we have? There are many places that reference genomes are available, though there are two main places to look for reference genomes ENSEMBL and National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI)

title: Exploring Public Sequencing Data
text:
ENSEMBL
A great place to look at high quality reference genomes is ENSEMBL. ENSEMBL contains information about genes, transcripts and further annotation. These can be retrieved at the genome, gene and protein level. It includes information on protein domains, genetic variation, homology, syntenic regions and regulatory elements.

To take a look at the human genome, click Homo sapiens. Many different types of data are available, including the full genome, annotation, regulatory element and known variants. To download the genome sequence, click Download DNA sequence. Each chromosome can be downloaded separately, the file named dna.toplevel.fa.gz at the end of the file contains the full genome.
To easily download the files onto a Linux machine, we can use the wget command. This command takes the link to the document online. To easily get the link to the file we want to download, right click the file and copy the link. The following should then download the file:
$ wget https://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/release-116/fasta/homo_sapiens/dna/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.dna.toplevel.fa.gz
If we go back to the genome overview, the annotation can be downloaded by clicking Download GTF or GFF3 to download the GTF annotation or GFF3 annotation file. For the GFF3 files, these again have a separate file for each chromosome.


 Challenge:

Download the GTF annotation file.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Using wget again to download the annotation, the following would be the command:
$ wget https://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/release-116/gtf/homo_sapiens/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.116.gtf.gz







 Challenge:

Extract both files.


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

We can use gunzip to unpack both files.
$ gunzip *.gz

title: Exploring Public Sequencing Data
text:
NCBI
NCBI is a central place for many different types of data. One of these places is the genome repository. Unlike ENSEMBL, these genomes are not always as highly curated and people can upload their own genomes to this repository easily. Genomes can be uploaded in different states of assembly, meaning that some of the genomes are only partially assembled and/or annotated.


 Challenge:

Go to the NCBI genome website, search for “Homo sapiens”. How many genomes are available for human? How many of these are complete genomes?
Hint: use the filters to select only complete genomes


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

From the amount of results, we can see that there are 2,574 genomes available for humans. Of these only 4 are considered to be complete.




The reference genome we previously explored at ENSEMBL is not part of the complete list. However, if we also accept genomes that are assembled to chromosome level, that reference genome (GRCh38.p14) now makes is on the list. The difference between complete and chromosome levels is that complete genomes should not contain any gaps, ambiguous bases or unplaced scaffolds. Chromosome level genomes can still contain some gaps and minor unplaced scaffolds. Both are generally considered good quality assemblies and can be used for different applications.

To download the genome, we can click the name of the assembly to go to the assembly page. Here more information can be found on the assembly and annotation of the genome.


 Challenge:

When was the first version of the human GRCh38.p14 genome uploaded?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Towards the bottom of the information page, we can find that the first upload was on the 22nd of February in 2010.



To download the genome, at the top of the page click FTP. There are multiple different files available for each download, lets look at and explain some of the most often used files. The following names are at the ends of the files:

genomic.fna.gz contains the genome sequence
genomic.gtf.gz contains gene descriptions and locations
genomic.gbff.gz contains a genbank file which contains both sequence and gene descriptions
protein.faa.gz contains protein sequences



 Key points

What are some essential things to consider when evaluating a reference genome?

The number of sequences within the assembly is important. The closer to the expected number of chromosomes, the better it should be. It is important to also take into account the full genome size and whether that is in line with what you expect for the reference genome.
In terms of annotation, it is often good to check how many genes have been annotated.

Depending on the application, generally its good to have a genome which is the species you are studying. However, if the genome for your specific species is not great, but a closely related species is high quality, it might be worth taking the related species.

title: Exploring Public Sequencing Data
text: Public data can be extremely helpful in a number of different applications. Whether testing new tools, writing applications, comparisons of data, it has become an essential source of data. Whenever publishing a scientific article, many papers will require the raw data to be made available online. Public data can be found in a selection of different places, with two central locations that most people will use to store raw sequence data, the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) and the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI). The data can contain reads for whole genome sequencing, gene expression or any other application sequencing can be used for, as well as data coming from different sequencers. We will take a look at the two main databases, how to search, download and finally quality check the data.

title: Exploring Public Sequencing Data
text:
ENA
ENA similar to SRA contains raw data. ENA covers more than just raw sequencing reads, it also contains assembly information and functional annotations.

Data within the archive is very similarly organised as SRA into several interconnected object types. Study represents the overall research project and contains information such as the study description, data ownership and release information. A Sample represents a biological sample included in a study. It can contain information such as the organism, sample type, collection location and other sample-specific metadata. An Experiment describes how a sample was prepared and sequenced. It links the Sample to the Study and contains information about the sequencing experiment, such as the library and sequencing platform. A Run represents an individual sequencing run and contains the raw sequencing reads generated by that run. Finally, an Analysis represents processed data derived from sequencing data, such as genome assemblies or sequence annotations. Below an overview of how the data is structured.






Search
The search can be limiting, however we can do text searches. Search for the term HeLa. Initially it might say no results were found, however results should start showing up shortly after. At the top of the screen, a bar will indicate if all results are given or if the search is still ongoing. Once the results are in, they are structured into different groups. To look at the full results for each group, click on link on the left.


 Challenge:

Take a look at all projects related to HeLa. How many projects are related to this term?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Click on Project on the left side of the screen. In total there are 2,515 projects related to HeLa.




Filtering the results within ENA is much more tricky than GEO or SRA. In general it is easier to search for data using IDs from publications. For many studies, data that is in NCBI will also be ENA. The link to ENA is often given in the form of a BioprojectID. Lets take a look at the study we looked at in SRA, but now in ENA.


 Challenge:

Take a look at the SRA results and find the BioProject. Search for PRJNA752995 in ENA. How many samples are available for this study in ENA?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Put the ID within the text search or in the accession search at the top of the page. In total there are 15 samples within this project.




The download for ENA is very straightforward. At the top of the FASTQ column there is a Download All button. If we press this button, a small script will be generated that we can run to download all the data. The script can be copied to server and run.
$ bash SCRIPT.sh
When downloading a study, you will only need to use one of the methods to download the data. Use the method whichever has your preference. Once the data is download, it is time for QC.

title: Public Data
text:
NCBI (GEO & SRA)
Previously, we looked at reference genomes in the NCBI dataset. Besides genomes, it also contains many different sets of tools and data that can come in handy in a multitude of situations, for now we will look raw sequencing data in GEO and SRA. GEO contains functional genomics experiments, which includes links to the raw data and the experimental results. SRA is the sequence archive that contains the raw reads. GEO can help us search for studies while SRA can help us search for specific data types.

GEO
GEO contains array and sequence-based expression data. To search in the GEO database, click “Search for Studies at GEO DataSets”. Now we can search the database for things that are of interest for us.


 Challenge:

Search for the famous cell line HeLa. How many results do you get? How many of these results were published in the last year? How many have a sample count between 100 and 200?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

To search, just type ‘HeLa’ in the search bar. Once the results are available, you can filter the results by publication date. There is also a filter for Sample count. If you do not see this option, click Show additional filters. Set the sample count to between 100 and 200.




Click any of the results to get more information, including a summary of experiment done, platforms used and links to data. We will take a look at downloading the data a little later on.

Often when looking for public data, the starting point will be a publication of interest. We have an example of a paper that might be of interest


 Challenge:

Open the paper. Take a look at the data availability. Can you find this dataset in GEO?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Generally towards the end of the paper there will be a section with Data Availability. In this case there are three different datasets for this paper within GEO. Either click the links or copy the ID and search for it in GEO to find the data.




Before going into how to download the data, lets take a look at SRA, as the download for these works the same way.


SRA
SRA is a repository for raw sequencing reads generated from a wide range of experimental approaches. These include RNA sequencing and other expression-related experiments, whole-genome and targeted sequencing, DNA methylation assays, Hi-C experiments, and many other high-throughput sequencing applications.
The data are organised into four main levels:

Study provides overarching information about the research project or investigation and groups related samples and experiments.
Sample describes the biological material from which the data were generated.
Experiment describes how the sample was prepared and sequenced, including details such as the library, sequencing technology, and experimental design.
Run represents an individual sequencing run and contains the raw sequencing reads generated during that run.

These levels are linked rather than strictly hierarchical. A single study can contain multiple samples, each sample can be associated with one or more experiments, and an experiment can have one or more sequencing runs.


 Challenge:

Same as for GEO, search for ‘HeLa’ in the search bar. How many results do you find? How do these results differ from GEO?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

SRA is different from GEO in the way that now we are looking at single run results, instead of being grouped into studies.




The data can be filtered on things like source or sequencing platform, this can help finding specific sample types.

title: Exploring Public Sequencing Data
text:
NCBI
Previously, we looked NCBI reference genomes. Besides genomes, it also contains many different sets of tools and data that can come in handy in a multitude of situations, for now we will look at experiments and associated raw sequencing data in Gene Expression Omnibus(GEO) and Sequence Read Archive (SRA). GEO contains functional genomics experiments, which includes metadata and experimental results. SRA is the sequence archive that contains the raw reads. GEO can help us search for studies and look at their results while SRA can help us search for specific data types.

GEO
GEO is a public repository for functional genomics data. It contains data from experiments such as gene expression profiling, RNA-seq, microarrays, epigenomics, and other high-throughput assays. To search in the GEO database, click “Search for Studies at GEO DataSets”. Now we can search the database for things that are of interest for us.


 Challenge:

Search for the famous cell line HeLa. How many results do you get? How many of these results were published in the last year? How many have a sample count between 100 and 200?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

To search, just type ‘HeLa’ in the search bar. Once the results are available, you can filter the results by publication date. There is also a filter for Sample count. If you do not see this option, click Show additional filters. Set the sample count to between 100 and 200.




Click any of the results to get more information, results can include a summary of experiment done, platforms used and links to data. GEO focuses on the biological experiment, associated samples and the resulting measurements.
Often when looking for public data, the starting point will be a publication of interest. We have an example of a paper that might be of interest


 Challenge:

Open the paper. Take a look at the data availability. Can you find this dataset in GEO?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

Generally towards the end of the paper there will be a section with Data Availability. In this case there are three different datasets for this paper within GEO. Either click the links or copy the ID and search for it in GEO to find the data.




GEO mainly focuses on the biological experiment, associated metadata and resulting measurements. When the underlying experiment involves sequencing, GEO records often provide links to the corresponding raw sequencing data. These raw sequencing reads are typically stored in the SRA.


SRA
SRA is a repository for raw sequencing reads generated from a wide range of experimental approaches. These include RNA sequencing and other expression-related experiments, whole-genome and targeted sequencing, DNA methylation assays, Hi-C experiments, and many other high-throughput sequencing applications.
The data are organised into four main levels:

Study provides overarching information about the research project or investigation and groups related samples and experiments.
Sample describes the biological material from which the data were generated.
Experiment describes how the sample was prepared and sequenced, including details such as the library, sequencing technology, and experimental design.
Run represents an individual sequencing run and contains the raw sequencing reads generated during that run.

These levels are linked rather than strictly hierarchical. A single study can contain multiple samples, each sample can be associated with one or more experiments, and an experiment can have one or more sequencing runs.


 Challenge:

Same as for GEO, search for ‘HeLa’ in the search bar. How many results do you find? How do these results differ from GEO?


Solution


Solution. 

 Solution:

SRA is different from GEO in the way that now we are looking at single run results, instead of an overview of a complete experiment.




The data can be filtered on things like source or sequencing platform, this can help finding specific sample types. Once a dataset of interest has been found, the next step is to download it. In SRA, this is a two step approach. The main thing we need to download is a runID.
Looking at the GEO results, at the bottom of the page there is a link to SRA Run Selector. This will lead to an overivew page, that contains a list of runID which can all be downloaded. As an example dataset, we will use a dataset which has a number of different HeLa cells sequenced separately. The data can be found here. Lets download the first record.
$ prefetch SRR15372746
Prefetch grabs all the information for a run. To download the fastq files related to the run, the following command can be used.
$ fasterq-dump SRR15372746/SRR15372746.sra
This will download the data for a single run. To download all the samples in dataset, the accession list can be downloaded from the SRA run page. An accession list will contain all the run IDs which are within a study. To then download the full set, this file can be used.
Note: You do not have to run these commands now
$ prefetch --option-file ACCESSIONLIST.txt
The SRA file will be downloaded for each one of the runs. To then download all the fastq files, a for loop can be used.
$ for i in */*.sra
    do
      fasterq-dump $i
    done
Again, this will take a while, however at the end of the command, all the data for the study should be downloaded.

title: Exploring Public Sequencing Data
text: Sequencing can be divided into two main branches: short read and long read sequencing. Each has different providers and specifications, which are described in the sections below.

title: Exploring Public Sequencing Data
text:
Short Reads
Short read sequencing, also known as second generation sequencing, involves breaking strands of DNA or RNA into smaller fragments, typically ranging from approximately 50–300 bp, and sequencing these fragments. Short read sequencing generally provides highly accurate reads at a relatively low cost, making it a widely used approach across a broad range of applications. Though there are several different providers, short read sequencing can create two main types of reads: single end or paired end reads.

Single end sequencing: As the name suggests, single end sequencing involves sequencing a DNA or RNA fragment from one end only. This is the simplest and most straightforward sequencing approach, but provides less information about the fragment compared with paired end sequencing.
Paired end reads: This involves sequencing the same fragment from both ends, generating two reads per fragment. These two fragments are revered to as forward (or R1) and reverse (or R2) reads. Depending on the size of the fragments, the forward and reverse read can overlap each other. Paired end sequencing is particularly useful for applications such as the detection of genomic rearrangements, gene fusions, novel transcripts, and other structural or transcriptomic features.




Figure 1: Visual representation of single end sequencing versus paired end sequencing. The red arrows indicate the forward (or R1) reads, the blue arrow represents the reverse (or R2) read.


Different platforms are available for short reads sequencing, these platforms employing different approaches to create short reads. In most cases, sequencing is based on sequencing by synthesis, sequencing by ligation, or sequencing by binding. The most used platforms are discussed below.

Illumina: Currently the dominant provider in the short read sequencing market and has been established in the field for many years. As a result, a large proportion of publicly available short read sequencing data has been generated using Illumina platforms.
Element Biosciences: Relatively new to the sequencing market that has grown rapidly in recent years. Element’s platforms offer highly accurate quality sequencing while aiming to provide a lower cost per read compared with established Illumina platforms.
Ultima Genomics: Another relatively new provider that is rapidly gaining momentum. Ultima focuses on highly scalable sequencing and aims to substantially reduce sequencing costs compared with traditional short read platforms.
MGI: A major sequencing provider with a particularly strong presence in Asia. Its platforms are also available in selected laboratories and sequencing facilities in Europe. It provides highly accurate short reads for a reduced cost compared to Illumina.

For a long time, Illumina dominated the short read sequencing field. Though the shift is slow, more and more labs are shifting to other platforms for short read sequencing needs.

title: Exploring Public Sequencing Data
text:
Long Reads
Long read sequencing, also known as third generation sequencing, focuses on generating longer reads than short read technologies. The two main platforms dominating the long read sequencing field are PacBio and Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT). Although both technologies are capable of generating reads that are considerably longer than those produced by short read platforms, they differ in their underlying approaches. Long read platforms generate single end reads.

PacBio focuses on generating highly accurate long reads, typically with read lengths around 10–25 kb. It combines long read sequencing with high accuracy by sequencing the same DNA molecule multiple times and generating a highly accurate consensus sequence. In addition to determining the DNA sequence, PacBio sequencing can provide information about the kinetics of nucleotide incorporation, which can be used to identify DNA modifications such as methylation without requiring a separate methylation-specific sequencing assay.
Oxford Nanopore has a strong emphasis on ultra-long reads and real-time sequencing. ONT can generate extremely long reads, with reads extending to megabase-scale lengths and, under specialised conditions, exceeding several megabases. The ability to generate ultra-long reads can be particularly valuable for resolving large structural variants, repetitive regions, complex genomic regions, and complete chromosome-scale assemblies. ONT sequencing can also detect DNA methylation and other base modifications directly from the sequencing signal. Another major advantage of ONT is its portability and flexibility. The company’s smallest sequencer, the MinION, is approximately the size of a USB stick and can be connected directly to a computer.

title: Exploring Public Sequencing Data
text:
Data files
Although sequencing technologies and the resulting data can differ between providers, the file formats used to deliver sequencing data are largely standardised. The two main file formats encountered in sequencing workflows are FASTQ and BAM files. Both formats contain information about the sequenced DNA or RNA and the quality of the sequencing data. FASTQ files contain the sequence reads together with a quality score for each base, whereas BAM files can contain more information about each read. Both file types will be explored during the course.
The quality of sequences is commonly represented using Phred quality scores. A Phred score provides an estimate of the probability that a base has been incorrectly identified, with higher scores indicating greater confidence in the base call. As a general rule, Q20 or higher is considered acceptable to good quality, while Q30 or higher is often used as a benchmark for high-quality sequencing data. However, what constitutes an acceptable quality score ultimately depends on the sequencing platform, application, and downstream analysis.

title: Exploring Public Sequencing Data
text: Each sequencing application has slightly different requirements and expectations regarding data quality. In this session, we will cover quality assessment, as well as discuss considerations specific to different types of sequencing data.

title: Exploring Public Sequencing Data
text:
Short Reads
For short-read sequencing, we will use FastQC and MultiQC to assess and summarise the quality of FASTQ files.

FastQC
To assess the quality of short read sequencing data, we will work with FASTQ files. FASTQ is a standardised file format that stores both the sequence information and the quality scores for each read. A single sequence entry in FASTQ format consists of four lines. The first line contains the sequence identifier or read name, the second line contains the nucleotide sequence, the third line is a separator, and the fourth line contains the quality score for each base, represented using Phred quality scores. An example of a single sequence can be found below.

A FASTQ file can contain millions of individual sequence reads, with each read represented by its own four-line entry. When working with paired-end sequencing data, each sample will typically have two FASTQ files. These files contain the reads generated from the two ends of each fragment and are usually referred to as the forward (R1) and reverse (R2) reads.
To be able to look at sequencing results, we will use the files from the sample we downloaded in the previous session.

Although FastQC provides useful indicators of potential issues that may need investigation, a red flag does not necessarily mean that the data are of poor quality. FastQC was originally developed for whole-genome sequencing data, and some of its checks may not be appropriate for other sequencing applications. For example, RNA-seq and metagenomic data can naturally produce warnings or failures because of their biological composition or library preparation. Below some of the common warnings given that might easily be explained.


 Notes


With Illumina sequencing, it is sometimes possible to see a short region of lower-quality bases at the beginning of the reads. This can be caused by low sequence diversity, where many reads start with the same or very similar bases. For example, in RNA-seq, reads may have a particular sequences because of the underlying biology or library preparation. A small decrease in quality at the start of the reads is therefore not necessarily a cause for concern.
With Illumina paired-end sequencing, it is common to see a gradual decrease in quality towards the end of the reads. As sequencing progresses, base-calling accuracy can decrease. This effect is often more pronounced in R2, as the reverse read is sequenced later in the process. Low quality bases at the ends of reads can often be removed using a read trimming tool, which we will cover in the ChIP-seq session.
The base composition at the beginning of reads, or even the entire read, may show variation. This can be expected for some sequencing applications. For example, RNA-seq libraries can have a biased sequence composition at the start of reads due to biological or library-preparation effects. Similarly, amplicon sequencing can target highly conserved regions, in those cases non-random base composition across the entire read can be expected.
The observed GC content may differ from the theoretical expectation for a particular organism or genome. This does not necessarily indicate a problem, particularly when the sample contains multiple species, as is common in metagenomic sequencing. Differences in genome composition between species can produce a broader or shifted GC-content distribution.
A high level of duplication is not necessarily a sign of poor quality data. In RNA-seq, highly expressed genes can naturally generate many reads with identical sequences. Similarly, in metagenomics, reads from a highly abundant species may be overrepresented in the dataset.
Adapter sequences can remain in the data after sequencing and may be detected by FastQC. Their presence is not necessarily unexpected, particularly when inserts are shorter than the sequencing read length. Adapter sequences can usually be identified and removed using a read trimming tool before downstream analysis.






MultiQC
In many projects, we need to assess the quality of multiple samples. Reviewing FastQC reports one by one is time consuming. MultiQC provides a simple way to combine the results from multiple FastQC analyses into a single report, allowing you to assess the overall quality of a study and easily identify samples that may require further investigation.
MultiQC is straightforward to use and can summarise results from dozens or even hundreds of samples in a single, easy-to-navigate report.
$ multiqc -o multiqc_results ./
The resulting data can be download again using a variaty of tools (FileZilla or Cyberduck), however we have prepared the data for all the samples within the study which can be explore through this link.
